PROFILE.name: Bharath Kumar Gaddam
PROFILE.heroBio: Hi, I’m {name}. I turn complex journeys into calm, conversion-ready experiences, from AI-powered design systems at Social Brands USA to product concepts inspired by Amazon, Google and Walmart.
PROFILE.statement: I bridge human needs, business goals and AI-powered products. From Hyderabad to Atlanta, one obsession has stayed the same: make complex things feel simple, and prove it with numbers.
PROFILE.aboutBio: I’m a multidisciplinary designer who also studies the systems behind the screen. After an MBA in Marketing & Digital Strategy and an M.S. in Business Analytics, I’m now pursuing a PhD in Information Technology & Infrastructure Management. My design work is backed by photography, video editing and drone cinematography.

CASES.title: Amazon AutoSphere
CASES.sub: A calmer way to buy a car on Amazon.
meta: Lead product designer, end-to-end UX & UI
CASES.note: Personal design concept. Amazon and related marks are trademarks of Amazon.com, Inc.
overview: Amazon already makes it easy to buy almost anything, but buying a car is still full of anxiety. Numbers are confusing, dealer conversations feel fragmented, and it’s hard to trust that a payment is fair.

For this concept I redesigned AutoSphere as a complete journey for buyers and dealers. Buyers get guided questions, clear monthly payments and a soft credit pre-check that feels safe. Dealers get a desktop workspace that pulls every lead, conversation and inventory issue into one place.
glance: Car buying on Amazon felt risky: unclear total cost, nervous credit checks, and nothing to track after reserving.
Research, flows, interaction and visual design for the buyer app, plus a desktop workspace for dealers.
Testers finished faster, understood payments better and felt confident booking a car from their phone.

wide.cap: The full buyer journey, from the first question to delivery tracking.

challenges: Online car buying felt risky for first-time shoppers.
Onboarding speaks to real scenarios like a first car, a family car or an upgrade. The entry screen explains what AutoSphere will and won’t do, and says up front that the pre-check is a soft pull.
Pricing and finance were scattered, so shoppers couldn’t see the monthly impact of their choices.
One payment screen with sliders for term and down payment, a live monthly amount, and a summary of price, estimated APR and amount due at signing.
After reserving a car, owners tracked everything through emails and dealer systems.
A dedicated Your Car area keeps delivery status, payments, service reminders and documents together inside Amazon.
stories: The journey opens with one question: what brings you here today? First-time buyer, shopping for a family, upgrading, luxury, or just browsing. Each answer tunes the guidance, cars and financing that follow, and there’s always a way to skip.

Shoppers choose how they think about money, total price or monthly payment, and a budget level. The app translates it into a real range, cars between $30,000 and $55,000 at around $650 a month, and says clearly that taxes and fees come later.

Results lead with a soft pre-check banner and quick filters for new, used and certified, buy or lease, SUV or EV. Each card shows the monthly estimate, delivery date, distance and dealer rating, with Prime Certified and best-match tags as trust signals.
The detail page pairs photography with a plain-language summary of why the car could suit this shopper, clearly labelled as AI-generated, next to the price, monthly estimate and a delivery promise.
Finance, lease and pay cash sit on one screen. Loan term and down payment move on sliders while the monthly figure updates, next to the estimated APR and amount due at signing.

Details come pre-filled from the Amazon account, and the screen says up front that this is a soft check that won’t affect the credit score. Results arrive as clearly labelled estimates, with the recommended plan explained.
Before anything is shared, a summary shows the selected car, payment option and dealer. After sending, a confirmation explains exactly what was shared and tracks the request inside Amazon.
An order summary, live tracking with an arrival window, and a guided checklist for body, glass, wheels and accessories, with photos and notes for anything that needs attention.
principles: Plain language anchored to real situations, with reassurance at every step of a high-value purchase.
Key money decisions live on one surface, always labelled as an estimate or a final lender offer.
Short, focused steps with visible progress, asking only for what is needed right now.
Payments, documents and service stay in the same experience after delivery.
process: Reviewed the current flow, read app reviews and interviewed first-time buyers, families and people upgrading to EVs, mapping emotions across the journey.
Defined the core problems, unclear total cost, nervousness about credit checks and losing track after reserving, and turned them into goals.
Rebuilt the end-to-end flow from a journey question through budget, matching, finance, dealer contact and delivery tracking.
High-fidelity screens in Figma on an Amazon-inspired system: cards, status chips and progress headers tuned for car buying.
Tested the prototype with a small group of shoppers, then simplified pre-check copy, clarified estimates and made the delivery checklist more visual.
a11y: Large touch targets and clear labels make key actions like saving a car, adjusting budget and starting a pre-check comfortable on any phone.
High-contrast colour pairs for text, chips and buttons keep the interface readable in bright light and for people with low vision.
Simple forms with inline errors and structured headings work well with screen readers and reduce mistakes in sensitive finance steps.
CASES.outcome: In usability sessions with first-time buyers and a dealer proxy, people finished the flow faster, understood payments better and felt more confident booking a car from their phone.

CASES.title: AutoSphere Dealer OS
CASES.sub: One workspace for every Amazon car lead.

hero.alt: Dealer OS lead inbox with summary tiles, a lead table and a lead detail panel

CASES.note: Personal design concept. Amazon and related marks are trademarks of Amazon.com, Inc.
overview: AutoSphere only works if dealers reply quickly and keep listings accurate. Today that work is spread across email, phone, spreadsheets and the dealer management system.

Dealer OS is the other half of the AutoSphere concept: a desktop workspace where a dealership sees every Amazon lead, replies in context and keeps inventory in sync, with the buyer’s pre-check and intent already attached.
glance: Leads arrive without context, replies are slow, and broken listings quietly disappear from Amazon.
Mapped the dealer side of the journey and designed the lead inbox, conversation view and inventory sync.
One place where every lead arrives with budget, intent and pre-check status, ready for a reply.
challenges: Dealers couldn’t tell which leads were serious.
Every lead row shows intent chips like hold, test drive or questions only, plus budget and pre-check status, so the warmest leads stand out.
Response time decides whether a buyer stays.
Summary tiles show new leads today, leads waiting for a reply against an Amazon target of under an hour, and test drives booked this week.
Listings broke without anyone noticing.
Inventory sync marks each listing as Live, Error or Draft and explains problems in plain language, like a listing hidden because it needs at least six photos.
stories: The inbox opens on three numbers that matter today, then a table of leads with vehicle, intent, budget, status and last activity. Selecting a row opens a side panel with the car, estimated payment, what the customer asked for and the next actions.

Replies happen next to everything the dealer needs: the customer’s request, system events like a completed soft pre-check and the pre-qualified amount, preferred contact and buying timeframe. Suggested actions keep the next step one click away.
Every vehicle shows price, payment band, listing status, sync health and views to leads. Errors sit inline with the fix, and dealers can run a sync, import a CSV or add a car by hand.
principles: A lead never arrives as just a name: budget, intent and pre-check travel with it.
Response targets and waiting leads are visible before anything else.
Problems come with the reason and the fix, in plain language.
Statuses and payment bands mirror what the buyer saw, so both sides talk about the same thing.
process: Followed a buyer request from the app to the dealership to find where context and time were lost.
Narrowed dealer work to three jobs: triage leads, reply in context and keep inventory healthy.
Designed tables, chips and side panels that hold a lot of information without feeling crowded.
Matched statuses, payments and events to the buyer app so both experiences tell one story.
a11y: Status never relies on colour alone: every chip and badge has a text label.
Tables keep clear column headers and generous row height for scanning and keyboard focus.
Error messages state the problem and the fix in the same line.
CASES.outcome: Dealer OS closes the loop on AutoSphere: buyers get fast, informed replies, and dealers spend their time selling instead of searching.

CASES.title: Orbit by Google
CASES.sub: Your whole Google day, in one place.

hero.alt: Two Orbit by Google phones on a plinth: the launch screen and the Good morning dashboard

CASES.note: Personal design concept. Google and related marks are trademarks of Google LLC.
overview: Orbit is a unified assistant that pulls everything from your Google ecosystem into one smart daily control center.

The home screen greets you by name, connects Gmail, Calendar, Meet, Drive and Maps, and surfaces what matters today: active projects, meetings, tasks due and unread email. Smart actions turn those signals into one-tap jobs, from clearing the inbox to paying the month’s bills.
glance: Daily life is split across Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Maps and Pay, and nothing connects the dots.
Concept, information architecture, interaction and visual design.
A daily control center with smart actions that turn signals into one-tap jobs.

wide.cap: The end-to-end flow, from launch to connected accounts and smart actions.

challenges: Important things hide in five different apps.
Orbit opens on one overview: connected services, today’s numbers and an “Ask Orbit anything” bar.
Bills get paid late because juggling them is tedious.
Smart Pay groups due bills, flags late-fee risk and suggests what to pay today.
Automation that moves money has to earn trust.
Clear confirmation screens, a visible split across payment methods and a 10-second undo.
stories: A morning dashboard, not another inbox
Instead of opening five apps, Orbit opens on a single overview: connected services along the top, today’s numbers in clear tiles, and an “Ask Orbit anything” bar for everything else.
Smart Pay: seven bills, one decision

Orbit lists every bill with its due date and late-fee risk, suggests how much to pay today to avoid fees, and splits payment across Google Pay methods. One confirmation pays five bills, with a 10-second undo.

The confirmation shows exactly what will happen: $1,800 across five bills, paid today at 2:05 PM because Orbit chose that time to avoid fees and overdrafts. The amount is split across a card, a checking account kept above $500 and the Google Pay balance.
principles: The day’s essentials fit on a single screen.
Orbit proposes actions and explains why before anything happens.
Every amount, account and time is visible before confirming.
Undo windows and autopay toggles keep people in control.
process: Listed the signals each Google app already holds and where they overlap in a normal day.
Designed around real moments like the morning check-in and paying bills.
Defined which jobs Orbit can safely bundle, starting with bills and inbox clean-up.
Built the screens on a Material-style system so Orbit feels at home on Android.
a11y: Primary actions like Pay and Undo use large, clearly labelled buttons.
Statuses are written out in words (“0 late fees · 0 overdrafts”), never shown by colour alone.
Totals come before details, which keeps the reading order clear for screen readers.
CASES.outcome: Orbit shows how an assistant can earn trust with money: show the reasoning, ask before acting and make every action easy to undo.

CASES.title: Walmart+ Membership
CASES.sub: From discount card to daily companion.
meta: Product designer: research, interaction, visual, system
CASES.note: Self-initiated concept inspired by Walmart+. Walmart marks belong to Walmart Inc.
overview: Walmart+ is positioned as the membership that saves busy families time and money, yet the experience feels fragmented between sign-up, savings tracking and everyday shopping.

I designed a mobile experience that treats Walmart+ as a daily companion rather than a discount card: a short onboarding that estimates your savings, an honest plan choice, and a shopping journey where membership value shows up at every tap.
glance: Members couldn’t see what they actually gain, and membership felt separate from everyday shopping.
Research, interaction design, visual design and the design system.
Testers understood the value before paying and could explain the plans in their own words.
challenges: Making membership value obvious in the first session.
Within seconds, members see a personal savings estimate and three perks that match everyday life, before any payment details.
Keeping pricing choices simple and honest.
Plans sit side by side with total cost, renewal timing and key perks in plain sight, with subtle emphasis instead of aggressive sales patterns.
Connecting benefits to everyday shopping.
Member prices sit next to regular prices, carts show savings for this order, and trips are planned around pickup, delivery or in-store.
stories: The welcome screen speaks like a helpful store associate: core benefits in plain language, one focused message per card, and a clear action that moves you forward.

A short quiz asks about grocery trips per month, spend per trip, how often you get deliveries and whether you buy fuel at Walmart. The result is a personal estimate, $412 a year in this example, broken into delivery fees, fuel and time saved with Scan & Go.
Annual and monthly plans sit side by side with total cost, savings versus monthly and a with-or-without comparison. The 30-day free trial and cancel-anytime terms are visible before sign-up.
A trip planner asks what the trip is for, when, and which store, then groups items by pickup or in-store with aisle numbers, so a quick shop really is quick.
Feels like Walmart, not a clone
Familiar Walmart blue with a warm accent, but a lighter, more open tone: generous white space, soft card shadows and a clean type scale that carries through every flow.
principles: Every key screen answers two questions in seconds: what can I do here, and what do I get.
Savings and perks appear before forms and payment, so the app feels on the member’s side.
Plain, friendly copy, clearly labelled actions and destructive choices that are hard to hit by mistake.
Shared grids, spacing tokens and reusable cards let new benefits plug in without losing clarity.
process: Simplified the Walmart palette: deep blue for trust and primary actions, warm yellow for savings moments, soft neutrals to keep screens calm.
A direct type hierarchy with generous line height and consistent spacing tokens, so dense screens scan in seconds.
Benefit cards, savings pills, banners, list rows and CTAs on one grid, so every feature feels like part of the same family.
Checked contrast on key actions and text, refined disabled and secondary states, and never let meaning rely on colour alone.
a11y: Primary buttons and important text meet WCAG AA contrast on white and soft grey.
Touch targets are at least 44 px with generous spacing, and primary actions stay in predictable places for one-handed use.
Icons always come with labels, and error, warning and success states combine colour with direct copy.
CASES.outcome: Testers understood the membership’s value before reaching payment, and could explain the difference between plans back in their own words.

CASES.title: Google Menu
CASES.sub: A food companion that understands your taste.
CASES.note: Personal design concept. Google is a trademark of Google LLC.
overview: Most food apps start with restaurants. People usually start with a craving: something warm, something spicy, something they had once and can’t name.

Google Menu is a concept for a food companion that starts with the dish. It understands your taste, your mood and your culture, lets you scan any dish with AI, and shows where to find it nearby, with the context you need to choose well.
glance: Choosing what to eat means jumping between maps, reviews and search, and unfamiliar dishes come with no context.
Concept, flows, interaction and visual design.
A dish-first discovery flow with AI scan, health context and saved collections.
challenges: People think in dishes; apps think in restaurants.
The home screen is organised around dishes and moments, with restaurants nearby as the second step.
Unfamiliar dishes are a gamble.
Every dish page explains what it is and adds tags like Popular nearby, AI Pick, Spicy and Best in evenings.
Health information is buried or missing.
Simple health insights give a calorie range and plain flags like high protein or high sodium.
stories: The home screen greets you by name and location, offers to scan any dish with the camera, and shows what’s trending and open now near you, with distance, time and rating.
A dish page for ramen describes it in one paragraph and adds context tags and health insights: roughly 450–700 kcal, high protein, high sodium, good for cold weather.
Categories like breakfast lead with a mood image and popular dishes near you, each showing how many places serve it.
Saved dishes, restaurants and collections live in one place, so the ramen you loved is easy to find again.
principles: Start from what people crave, then show where to get it.
Short descriptions and tags answer “what is this?” fast.
Ranges and simple flags instead of false precision.
Saving is one tap and collections keep favourites organised.
process: Mapped when people decide what to eat: commutes, breaks, late evenings, travel.
Rebuilt navigation around dishes and moods, with restaurants as the second layer.
Placed AI where it saves effort: scanning a dish and picking dishes for you.
Large food photography, soft cards and clear tags in a clean, Google-like interface.
a11y: Text over photography sits on a dark gradient for readable contrast.
Tags pair an icon with a word, never an icon alone.
Distances, times and ratings are written out, not only implied by icons.
CASES.outcome: Google Menu reframes food discovery around the dish, so deciding what to eat starts with the craving instead of a list of restaurants.

CASES.title: Social Brands USA
CASES.sub: One design system for 8+ product lines.

hero.alt: Social Brands USA: 8+ product lines, one system

CASES.note: More visuals coming soon. Selected packaging and campaign work below.
overview: Social Brands USA runs a portfolio of consumer products, each with its own packaging, campaigns and online presence. As the line-up grew, every launch was being designed almost from scratch.
I joined in Atlanta to bring it under one system: AI-powered design systems and packaging across 8+ product lines, so new products launch faster and look like they belong together.
impact: less time to create new components
glance: Many product lines, many looks, and every launch starting from zero.
Design system architecture, packaging, campaign creative and brand strategy.
More consistent design, faster production and lifts in sales, retention and engagement.
challenges: Every product line had its own rules.
A shared foundation of type, colour, layout and components that each brand extends instead of reinventing.
Packaging was rebuilt for every SKU.
Reusable packaging templates and dielines, so new flavours and sizes start from a proven layout.
Campaigns needed volume without losing quality.
AI-assisted production inside the system, so seasonal campaigns stay on-brand at speed.
stories: Dielines, dimensions and print-ready layouts designed as a family, so each SKU inherits the structure and only changes what makes it unique.
Holiday and promotional creative built from the same system, from count displays to hero product shots.
Offers and campaign artwork adapted across formats and channels without redrawing the brand each time.
Each line keeps its own personality while sharing the structure underneath.
principles: Decide the rules once, then design products inside them.
Every template is built for print and e-commerce from day one.
Consistency and speed are tracked, not assumed.
process: Collected live packaging, ads and pages to see where brands had drifted apart.
Defined type, colour, grids and components as the shared layer.
Turned packaging and campaign layouts into reusable templates.
Brought AI tools into production for imagery and variations, reviewed against the system.
Moved product lines onto the system one launch at a time.
CASES.outcome: A portfolio of brands that launch faster and look like they belong together.

CASES.title: Blue Dart Express
CASES.sub: The first enterprise design system, across 50+ territories.

hero.alt: Blue Dart: 50+ territories on one design system

overview: Blue Dart is one of India’s leading express logistics companies and part of the DHL Group. Regional teams across the country were producing their own materials, and the brand looked different from one territory to the next.
I led the company’s first enterprise-scale design system, giving 50+ territories one visual language and a faster way to produce on-brand work.
glance: Every territory made its own materials, so the brand looked different everywhere.
Led the design system: foundations, templates, guidelines and rollout.
73% higher brand recognition and turnaround cut from two weeks to five days.
challenges: 50+ territories, 50+ versions of the brand.
One documented system of colour, type, layout and imagery for every region.
Requests took two weeks to turn around.
Ready-made templates and clear guidelines cut turnaround to five days.
Local teams needed freedom without breaking the brand.
Flexible templates with locked brand elements and editable local content.
stories: National campaigns, like the rename of Dart Plus to Bharat Dart, shared the same visual language as every regional piece.
Regional teams worked from shared templates, changing local content while the brand stayed intact.
Rules written for the people producing the work, with examples of what to do and what to avoid.
principles: Every territory speaks with the same voice.
Self-serve layouts beat waiting in a queue.
process: Gathered materials from across territories to see how far they had drifted.
Set colour, type, imagery and layout rules.
Built templates for the most-requested formats.
Introduced the system region by region with guidelines and examples.
CASES.outcome: One brand across 50+ territories, produced faster by the people closest to customers.

CASES.title: Sri Sai Logistics
overview: My first full-time design role. Sri Sai Logistics needed a steady flow of marketing material, from print collateral to social posts and digital ads, and every piece went through long rounds of revisions.
Alongside designing 150+ assets, I fixed the process around them, which cut revision cycles by 40% and improved campaign performance by 28%.
glance: Lots of marketing work, slow approvals and inconsistent results.
Design and digital marketing: collateral, social and ads, plus the workflow around them.
40% fewer revisions and 28% better campaign performance.
challenges: Vague briefs meant endless revisions.
Simple brief templates captured goals, audience and must-haves before design started.
Every asset looked a little different.
Reusable layouts and brand rules kept collateral consistent.
No feedback loop from results.
Campaign results fed back into the next round of creative.
stories: Daily production taught me hierarchy, typography and speed, the foundations I still use in every project.
Fixing the process, not just the pixels
The biggest win wasn’t a single design. It was a clearer brief and review process that let good work ship faster.
principles: Clear goals before the first pixel.
Consolidated feedback instead of endless loops.
Let results shape the next asset.
process: Goals, audience and must-haves agreed before design.
Used campaign data to improve the next asset.
CASES.outcome: Proof that fixing the process can matter as much as the design itself.

CASES.title: Portfolio CMS

hero.alt: The CMS project editor with tabs for general info, media, content blocks, page sections and stats

overview: I wanted a portfolio I could update without touching code, so I designed and built my own content management system.

Every section of the site, from the hero to the case studies, lives in a database and is edited from an admin panel. Sections can be reordered or hidden, case studies are built from content blocks, and media lives in one library.
glance: Website builders were either too rigid or too generic for detailed case studies.
Product design, content modelling and front-end development.
A custom CMS with 50+ content tables powering the live site.
challenges: Case studies need more than a title and a gallery.
Projects are edited in tabs for general info, media, content blocks, page sections and stats.
The homepage should change without a redeploy.
Homepage sections are stored with visibility and order, so the layout is edited from the admin.
Media gets messy fast.
One media library feeds every section and case study.
stories: A tabbed editor for title, client, role, description, status and categories like App Design, Branding, Motion Graphics, Packaging and Print Design.
Hero variants, galleries, showcases and testimonials are separate sections that can be turned on, off and reordered.
Postgres tables, storage for media and authentication for the admin, with a React and Vite front end styled with Tailwind CSS.
principles: Everything on the page is structured, so it can be reused and reordered.
Tabs mirror how a case study is actually written.
Full control over design, speed and data.
process: Listed every piece of content on the site and turned it into tables.
Designed the editor around how I actually update projects.
React with Vite and Tailwind CSS on the front end, Supabase underneath.
Published real case studies with it and smoothed out friction along the way.
CASES.outcome: Designing the tool I use every day made me sharper at designing tools for other people.

CASES.title: AirPods Pro reveal

hero.alt: AirPods Pro earbuds floating over the product name on a dark stage

CASES.note: Personal study. AirPods and Apple are trademarks of Apple Inc.
overview: Product pages live or die on the first few seconds of scrolling. This study explores how a launch page can feel cinematic without losing the information people came for.
The earbuds float over the product name on a dark stage, then motion, type and depth carry the visitor from the reveal into the details.
glance: Make a product page feel like a film while staying fast and readable.
A scroll-driven reveal where scrolling sets the pace.
stories: A dark stage, oversized type and the product in front of it. The type sets the scale and the product breaks the frame, so depth reads instantly.
Each scroll step moves the story forward: reveal, rotate, then detail. Motion is tied to scroll position, so visitors control the pace.
Animation stops when information starts. Specs, price and buttons sit still and stay readable.
principles: The visitor’s scroll drives the story.
A single strong reveal beats many small effects.
Animation ends where the information begins.
Only transforms and opacity animate, so it stays fluid.
process: Sketched the page as frames before any animation.
Tuned easing and pacing in a motion tool before moving to the browser.
Translated the timing into scroll-linked animation.
Tightened pacing so the reveal never delays the content.
a11y: Respects reduced-motion settings with a static version of the page.
Text never sits on moving imagery without a solid backdrop.
CASES.outcome: The best motion on a product page is one strong moment, followed by clear information.

CASES.title: Nike Alphafly 3
CASES.sub: A product page that restages itself.

hero.alt: Nike Alphafly 3 product page with a colourway picker and size grid

CASES.note: Personal study. Nike and Alphafly are trademarks of Nike, Inc.
overview: Colour is the first thing runners choose, yet most product pages only swap a small thumbnail when you pick one.
This study makes the colourway the hero: choosing one restages the whole shoe shot, with size selection right below in a clear grid.
glance: Make choosing a colourway feel like the product itself.
A page where the main choice is also the main visual.
stories: The large shoe shot changes with the chosen colourway, so the decision and the image are the same thing.
A size grid sits right under the colour picker, so both decisions happen without scrolling.
Navigation and copy step back so the shoe and the choice stay in focus.
principles: Selections change the hero, not a thumbnail.
process: Compared how leading sneaker pages handle colour and size.
Put the picker and size grid under one hero.
Designed the restaging transition between colourways.
Refined spacing and type around the product.
a11y: Colour options carry names, not just swatches.
Size buttons are large and keyboard-reachable.
CASES.outcome: When the main choice is also the main visual, the page sells the product by itself.
